title: Paraparticles intrinsically exhibit Hardy-space breakdown
abstract: The memory kernel of an open quantum system obeys Kramers--Kronig (KK) relations if and only if its Laplace transform is analytic in the upper half-plane -- a property known as Hardy-space analyticity. Here we show that non-unitary exchange statistics, the defining property of paraparticles, intrinsically breaks Hardy-space analyticity. The metric $η$ that guarantees a real closed-system spectrum for these particles necessarily differs from the physical Born inner product ($\|η- I\|_F / \|I\|_F = 0.51$) -- a mathematical consequence of the R-matrix's non-unitarity, not a parameter choice. This metric is a "shadow metric": Schur's lemma forces it to commute with every bilinear observable, making the distortion physically invisible in the closed system. But when the paraparticle is coupled to a bath, any coupling operator that lies outside the symmetry algebra -- that is, any interaction that sees the internal flavour structure -- exposes the distortion. The memory kernel then develops upper-half-plane poles at coupling $g_c \approx 0.1$, breaking standard dispersion relations before the closed-system spectrum complexifies. Fermions and bosons, whose exchange is unitary ($η= I$ as an analytic fact of the canonical anticommutation algebra), are immune at any coupling, because there is no distortion to expose. The violation is intrinsic: it distinguishes non-unitary exchange statistics from ordinary particle statistics at the level of the memory kernel's analytic structure.
summary: The paper proves that particles with non-unitary exchange statistics ('paraparticles') fundamentally break a mathematical property called Hardy-space analyticity in their memory kernel when interacting with an environment. This breakdown is exposed by interactions sensitive to the particle's internal structure, distinguishing it sharply from standard fermions and bosons.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether non-unitary exchange statistics, characteristic of 'paraparticles,' intrinsically violate Hardy-space analyticity in the memory kernel describing open quantum system dynamics.
main_result: Paraparticles break this mathematical symmetry when coupled to an environment via interactions outside the system's symmetry algebra. This breakdown is intrinsic and occurs at coupling strengths where the total Hamiltonian remains spectrally real.
method: The analysis relies on examining the Kramers-Kronig relations, which require Hardy-space analyticity of the memory kernel derived from the Nakajima-Zwanzig projection formalism.
model_or_system: The model involves paraparticles with non-unitary exchange statistics coupled to an environment (bath). The dynamics are analyzed by comparing the required 'shadow metric' ($\eta$) against the physical Born inner product ($I$).
key_observables: Hardy-space analyticity of the memory kernel $	ilde{K}(z)$, which is diagnosed by searching for poles in the Upper Half-Plane (UHP) corresponding to Right-Half-Plane (RHP) eigenvalues of the projected generator $QLQ$.
important_parameters: The coupling strength ($g$), particularly noting a breakdown point near $g_c \approx 0.1$, and the ratio $\lVert\eta - IVert_F / \lVert IVert_F = 0.51$ for paraparticles.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the failure of Hardy-space analyticity, signaled by UHP poles in $	ilde{K}(z)$, provides a definitive signature of non-unitary statistics when coupled to an environment.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how coupling breaks the 'Schur shield' protecting the closed system dynamics, causing UHP poles in the memory kernel ($\max 	ext{Re}(\lambda Q_{LQ})$) even when the total Hamiltonian ($H_{tot}$) spectrum remains real at strong couplings.
paper_structure:
The paper builds a mathematical argument by first establishing the necessary conditions (Hardy-space analyticity $\iff$ KK relations) and then demonstrating how non-unitary statistics ($\eta 
eq I$) violates these conditions when an external interaction probes the internal flavor structure, contrasting this with unitary systems (fermions/bosons).
why_interesting: This work provides a deep mathematical link between fundamental quantum statistics (unitarity of exchange) and the analytic properties of open system dynamics, suggesting that spectral signatures can reveal underlying non-unitary physics even when standard energy measurements appear normal.
